items.title: care is contagious
items.author: Jodi Wilson
items.description: Apologies for my absence last week. I’d spent the entire week feverish and mostly in bed, and had very little to say. Of course I believe in a good, therapeutic whinge but I didn’t want to add any of my own misery to your inbox. We could all do without a fever and the associated malaise, lack of appetite (I couldn’t even drink my beloved coffee!) and sinus-infected aftermath, but when you’re forced to be still and quiet for days on end, you do get a lot of thinking done. I tried not to think too much about my detailed plans that had well and truly disintegrated (really regret writing that essay) and instead focus on the necessary mind-wandering that was happening as I drifted in and out of daydreams. I was reminded, yet again, that a simple dinner of rice, broth and pak choi cooked in garlic and chilli oil feels indulgent, that soup in the freezer is the greatest gift you can give yourself, that you should always have a well-stocked cupboard of nurofen and panadol and tissues and lozenges; lemons in the fruitbowl and herbal tea in the kitchen. You feel incredibly rich when you have access to these small comforts. Subscribe now I call it ‘taking care of future-you’ which is a clunky sentence but the sentiment is clear. I know you may be thinking ‘it’s hard enough to take care of myself in the moment!’ and I agree that yes, it is hard, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth doing. I love convenience as much as the next person – ease is always preferable - but I feel like it’s flattened so much of our lives, and removed the friction that reminds us how good it feels to be on the other side of something difficult. To overcome an obstacle, even if it’s a slight detour, can be a reset, of sorts. But I can hold two truths at once and agree with Bill McKibben who, in his recent opinion piece for the New York Times, discussed the fact that we are not built for this current world. It’s US-centric but relevant to us all, noting the climate crisis and AI dominance alongside unstable political leadership as three main factors informing our prolific uncertainty and rising anxiety; our deep, deep exhaustion. It’s the final paragraph that resonates most: “Because if human survival and economic resilience are important goals, so is a world calm enough to meet the needs of the human nervous system. We can’t keep on like this — it’s simply inhuman. We’re creating a world that’s fit only for something artificial.” The question is: how can you create reliable calm in your own small world? Every piece of advice about how to weather this current onslaught of overwhelm is to go out into your community and find solace with other people. It’s true: we have always existed together, and our current isolation is only exacerbating our neuroses. But I also believe that learning to take care of yourself – despite it all – is a genuinely good and practical first step. Care is contagious. It’s also accessible to you right now. I’m hesitant to use the word ‘cope’ because it alludes to the fact that we’re just getting by, and while there may be some truth to the matter, I prefer to take the more-optimistic route: when you make care a priority in your life, it becomes an reliable comfort that allows you to simply be. Care creates space for you to dial down the noise and threats of the world and allows you to focus on what remains, which is often many beautiful, heart-healing things. Now is precisely the time for beauty and comfort, and for indulging in both. I’ve noticed over the past few weeks of illness, that there is still a fight in my head about resting and working. I know that rest allows me to heal better (not necessarily faster) and that I cannot write when my head is heavy and my thoughts are slow. But I’m also aware that accepting where I’m at - honouring the season I’m in - is a genuine form of care. But gosh it takes practice, and kind self-talk, and mostly trust that rest will eventually help the work get done, and that work isn’t all of life anyway. Around and around I go, slowly getting closer to the truth of the matter. Our brain loves immediate gratification (it’s one reason why we’re addicted to our phones and swept up in consumer culture) and by seeking this, we numb out from normal life - from both the grief and the joy of it. Care requires our focus and attention, which means at the beginning we are honing in on what’s uncomfortable and tetchy in both mind and body. Your immediate reaction may be to leap away and get distracted, which is why care also requires you to forgive yourself. Forgive myself of what? you may ask, and to that I say: forgive yourself of all the ‘shoulds’, of the ingrained ideals of perfection, of any thought that prevents you from caring for yourself in meaningful ways. A poem I read a few weeks ago: Clearing - Martha Postlewaite Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published Do not try to serve the whole world or do anything grandiose Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published Instead, create a clearing in the dense forest of your life and wait there, patiently Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published until the song that is yours alone to sing falls into your open cupped hands and you recognise and greet it. Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published Only then will you know how to give yourself to the world so worthy of rescue. Never in my life have I reached for poetry like I am at the moment, perhaps because the words are so acutely considered, and the arrangement of them - deliberate and profound - is art in itself. And then of course, there is the white space on the page, which as Elizabeth Strout says is a ‘pragmatic helpfulness’. It says: come, be, you don’t need to strive here. Care is the white space in your days. It’s where you turn up, just as you are, and allow yourself to be in the quiet. It is your clearing in the dense forest of life. This isn’t about ‘wellness’, it’s about being human - imperfectly, wonderfully and gently yourself, doing all the unfussy and boring things that settle you in the moment. And then? Talk about care to the people in your life - what it looks like for you and how you prioritise it in your days. Let it be contagious. Leave a comment Practising Simplicity is coming in paperback Look at that cheery yellow cover! First published in 2022, Practising Simplicity details the story of my family’s decisions to sell most of what we owned and travel Australia in a caravan. It was an odd choice for someone like me to make; I’m an anxious person who will always favour predictability, and who somehow made the spontaneous decision to spend our entire life savings on a 4WD and caravan (having never camped or caravanned before). I really did question myself in the eight months it took us to get organised but I continued to think about 80-year-old me (my late future-self) and I intuitively knew that if I was looking back on my life I’d probably regret not making this huge leap. Really, it was a series of small steps and brave decisions and when we were eventually on the road, an unravelling of all the obligations and expectations that I had taken on as a mother of 4. Practising Simplicity is the story of my emotional journey - of living with less, figuring out what matters and making decisions accordingly. It’s an illustrated book, too - each page features one of my photos that I took over the 2.5 years we were travelling in a 24ft van with only the essentials. I’m also well aware that without the success of A Brain That Breathes – which I largely attribute to longstanding readers like you – Practising Simplicity wouldn’t be getting reprinted. Authors need their readers and I’m grateful that you’re mine. You can pre-order now through your local independent bookstore (preferably) or online: Booktopia Pre-order Amazon Pre-order other things I’ve been nominated for the board of the Australian Society of Authors. If you’re a paying member you have until early November to place your vote. I’m passionate about advocating for authors and illustrators as our work is threatened by AI and copyright infringement. I also believe we should be doing everything we can to protect the arts and support artists because when we’re grieving and anxious, and when we feel hopeless, many of us find solace in books - they are our comfort, our care and our life force. Designer Elizabeth Suzann, known for her dedication to slow fashion, is taking ‘slow’ one step further and starting a sheep farm so she can grow her own fiber. ‘The world is crazy, this industry is in shambles, so fuck it - why not just try stuff?’ I love this attitude: why not just try? Pickle slaw for summer? Oh, yes please! I read a lot over the past few weeks: Switzy by Emma Cline was the ideal read while feverish and I’m surprised it didn’t make the Booker shortlist, Phantom Days by Angela O’Keefe is short, sharp and clever, The Sun was Electric Light by Rachel Morton is so unique in its voice that it’s still lingering my mind (it’s on the shortlist for the Barbara Jefferis Award), May We Feed The King by Rebecca Perry was best in the first half, People Skills by Nina Kenwood is the intelligent rom-com we all need and a reliable antidote to whatever may be challenging in your life, The Salt Stones by Helen Whybrow is a meandering story of a shepherd’s life and proof that a sense of hopelessness is almost always rectified by nature (and/or nature writing). I’m now in the middle of Neha Kale’s Foreign Return, Amy Matthews’ The Treasure House and Caitlin Moran’s How to be Hopeful. This week I plan to buy American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee (if you haven’t read Pachinko, please do!) and The Strangers by Naomi Alderman. I will also likely browse the poetry section of the bookshop. When in doubt, open a book! Till next week, take care x buy A Brain That Breathes Practising Simplicity is a reader-supported publication.
